body:
Persian as a language of imperial culture

Persian occupied a prominent position in Mughal administration, literature and courtly life. Although the Mughal rulers had Central Asian origins and Babur wrote in Turkish, Akbar made Persian the leading language of the imperial court and administration.

Knowledge of Persian became important for officials, accountants, secretaries, scholars and writers. Its vocabulary and literary conventions also influenced several Indian languages.

The Mughal court did not operate in complete separation from local cultures. Persian was used by people whose home languages included Hindavi and various regional languages. Interactions between Persian and North Indian speech traditions contributed to the historical development of Urdu.

Akbarnama and Ain-i Akbari

Abu'l Fazl composed the Akbarnama under Akbar's patronage. Its first 2 books provided a historical narrative, while the third, the Ain-i Akbari, described imperial administration and the wider society and economy.

The Ain-i Akbari was completed in 1598. It contains information about revenue arrangements, crops, prices, administrative divisions, officials and cultural practices.

The work is especially useful for distinguishing a historical chronicle, which narrates events, from an administrative compendium, which systematically describes institutions and conditions.

Persian translations of Sanskrit works

Akbar supported translation projects that brought Indian literary and religious works into the Persian-language environment of the imperial court.

The best-known example is the Razmnama, the Persian version of the Mahabharata. The Ramayana was also translated into Persian during his reign.

These projects are examples of interaction among scholars, translators, scribes and painters from different cultural backgrounds. They contributed to the exchange of literary ideas rather than eliminating the original-language traditions.

The imperial kitabkhana

The kitabkhana was the centre for storing and producing manuscripts at the Mughal court. Although the word may be translated as library, it was also an active manuscript workshop.

Creating an illustrated manuscript required the combined work of different specialists:

  • Paper makers: Prepared the sheets on which manuscripts were written and illustrated.
  • Scribes and calligraphers: Copied the text in carefully formed writing.
  • Painters: Illustrated scenes and decorated manuscript pages.
  • Gilders: Added gold and other ornamental details.
  • Bookbinders: Assembled and protected the completed manuscript.

Calligraphy was particularly valued. Nastaliq, a flowing style of Persian writing, was among the important scripts used at the Mughal court.

Persianate culture and Indian traditions

Persianate culture refers to the wider cultural world in which Persian language, literary conventions, courtly practices and artistic forms played major roles. It was not confined to Iran and was not identical to religious identity.

In Mughal India, Persianate court culture interacted with Indian languages, artistic traditions, architectural methods and social practices. This interaction can be seen in manuscript illustration, translations, miniature painting, garden planning and monumental architecture.

Gujarat's place in this synthesis

Gujarat contributed to the wider Mughal world through its commercial networks and established craft traditions. Surat connected the empire with overseas markets, Ahmedabad supported manufacturing and trade, and the region's earlier Indo-Islamic architectural forms formed part of the broader environment from which Mughal architecture developed.

These connections illustrate the relationship between regional traditions and imperial patronage. The Mughal court drew upon skills and forms that existed across the subcontinent, while its wealth and prestige helped circulate selected artistic practices more widely.

Connecting economy and culture

Economic resources and cultural production were closely connected. Agricultural revenue helped finance the imperial establishment, while merchants and artisans supplied goods, materials and expertise. Wealthy patrons could then commission buildings, paintings, manuscripts, textiles and other skilled work.

The result was not one uniform culture. Mughal achievements emerged from interactions among imperial institutions, local communities, regional artistic schools and international commercial and cultural contacts.

Prelims focus

  • Baburnama: Babur; originally Chagatai Turkish.
  • Humayun Nama: Gulbadan Begum.
  • Akbarnama and Ain-i Akbari: Abu'l Fazl.
  • Ain-i Akbari: third book of the Akbarnama, completed in 1598.
  • Razmnama: Persian translation of the Mahabharata under Akbar.
  • Trap: Kitabkhana was both a manuscript collection and a centre of manuscript production.
